titleStmt.title: Digital Methodology
An Overview of Data Modeling, Technologies, and Interfaces in edition humboldt digital

editionStmt.p: Dumont, Stefan: Digital Methodology . An Overview of Data Modeling, Technologies, and Interfaces in edition humboldt digital. In: edition humboldt digital, hg. v. Ottmar Ette. Berlin-Brandenburgische Akademie der Wissenschaften, Berlin. Version 12 vom 08.06.2026. URL: https://edition-humboldt.de/v12/

editorialDecl.p: Art und Weise der Transkribition, Annotation und Kodierung der Texte sind in den Richtlinien der edition humboldt digital umfassend dokumentiert, siehe https://edition-humboldt.de/richtlinien/. Die Schemata sind als ODD- und RNG-Dateien unter https://github.com/telota/ediarum.AVHR.data-model bereitgestellt.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: The “edition humboldt” is published as a hybrid edition, but with a “digital first” approach: all edited texts and scholarly articles are first published under an open license at edition humboldt digital.Vgl. Kraft/Dumont 2020. For more on the hybrid concept of the edition, see also Kraft 2018. The “edition humboldt digital” follows a “digital paradigm,” as defined by Patrick Sahle (2017): thus, the ehd is not only accessible online and based—in accordance with the “single source” principle—on TEI-XML, but also features numerous pieces of information and functions that cannot be reproduced in print without loss of information.

This article aims to introduce the fundamental digital methodology of the edition humboldt digital. The article should therefore be viewed in the context of the required transparency in editorial practice (such as the editorial guidelines or the respective introductions to the edited texts). However, it focuses on the genuinely digital aspects of the edition—namely, the data model and software, web design, reused external data and services, as well as the interfaces and publication of the data. This article is intended as an initial overview and will be supplemented by further content. Notable examples include the editorial guidelines, Kraft 2018, Kraft/Dumont 2020, and Dumont et al. 2026.. Several individuals with varying responsibilities have been and continue to be involved in the development of the ehd; their names can be found in the “Project Team” section.

div.head: Data Model
div.p: This section provides an overview of the edition’s data model. Comprehensive documentation of the data model is available in the edition guidelines. For background on the data model (e.g., the use of “cascading standards” or the edition levels), see also Dumont et al. 2026.

div.head: Historical Sources
div.p: The metadata and texts of the works to be edited (travel diaries, documents, and letters) are encoded according to the guidelines of the Text Encoding Initiative (TEI). In doing so, ediarum.BASE.edit is used to largely adhere to the base format of the German Text Archive (DTABf) (Haaf/Geyken/Wiegand 2015), which has been extended—among other things—for the encoding of handwritten texts as part of this editorial project (Haaf/Thomas 2018). For a few project-specific requirements, additions and extensions to the tag set have been made that are compliant with the TEI guidelines. These extensions primarily address project-specific requirements arising from the source material, such as the markup of measurements or inserted or pasted-in notes. However, when making extensions to the DTABf data model, care was taken to ensure that they align as closely as possible with its existing structure. Thus, in many cases, no new elements or attributes were added; instead, only attribute values were supplemented.

All names of people, places, and institutions, as well as bibliographic references in the source texts (and their metadata), are linked in the texts to their respective index entries. Similarly, dates in the diaries are encoded and can thus be automatically linked to the next chronological entry in the timeline.

div.head: Accompanying Texts
div.p: All other texts, such as the introductory research articles on the diary fragment “Isle de Cube. Antilles en général,” were also recorded in TEI-XML in accordance with the base format of the German Text Archive.

div.head: Index
div.p: The indexes for people, places, and institutions, as well as the glossary, are processed and maintained in TEI-XML. Each entry has its own unique and permanent ID. In addition to the basic data for an entry, a brief description is also provided.

The entries are also assigned one or, where applicable, several URIs from various authority files, provided an entry exists there. This enables projektübergreifende identification of the people, places, and institutions both within the ehd itself and when using the interfaces and data publications (see also Stadler 2012 regarding authority files in editions). For person entries, the GND is primarily used; alternatively or additionally, Wikidata is also used. VIAF was previously used as well, but this approach was abandoned due to the instability of the VIAF API and uncertain future prospects—Wikidata now appears to be the better alternative here. For places, on the other hand, URIs from the free location database GeoNames are used, as it provides extensive global coverage and entries can be supplemented by the project itself as needed. For example, a few locations missing from GeoNames (such as the former sites of the Berlin Observatory) were added there.

In addition, as part of the project, the catalog entries for 25 editions (letters, documents, diary excerpts) of Alexander von Humboldt research published between 1973 and 2016 were retro-digitized and made available. The catalog information for the printed editions is part of the series *Beiträge zur Alexander von Humboldt-Forschung*, originally published by Akademie-Verlag and later by De Gruyter, edited by the Alexander von Humboldt Research Center (1970–2014) of the BBAW.
Links to other index entries and the edited materials are automatically extracted from the database using the ehd-ID.

div.head: Humboldt’s Reference Sigla
div.p: Alexander von Humboldt’s manuscripts sometimes contain so-called sigla—that is, letter combinations that link various documents, letters, and diary entries to one another. These sigla were not only transcribed but also entered into a separate TEI-XML register and linked to the corresponding text passages. This allows the relationships to be traced within the digital edition as well.

div.head: Plant Index
div.p: No separate entries are created in TEI-XML register files for the plant index (as is the case with the other registers). Instead, the scientific plant names in the edited texts are annotated using the appropriate TEI markup, normalized where necessary, and then automatically extracted. The plant index is thus generated entirely dynamically. For each distinct plant name, the citations in the texts are listed and automatically linked to various taxonomic databases (see below, section “Global Indexes for Scientific Names”).

However, since Version 10 (1 December 2024), the plant index—which is inherently dynamic—is additionally generated automatically as TEI-XML (including internal and external references). This ensures that the plant index can continue to be included with data publications in the future. See also Section 3.2 at Dumont et al. 2026.

div.head: Drawings and Sketches
div.p: Since Version 9, a virtual “index” has provided an overview of drawings and sketches by Humboldt or other contemporaries found in the edited texts. Similar to the plant index, it is automatically compiled from the illustrations tagged with figure.

div.head: Bibliography
div.p: The edition’s bibliography is maintained in the reference management software Zotero. The publicly accessible Zotero group enables collaborative maintenance of the data and can be accessed by anyone interested—including in various citation styles and export formats (see below).

div.head: Documentation
div.p: The data model is documented in DITA, specifically in the DITA files of ediarum.BASE.manual. This allows for synergies and documents any specifications or modifications relative to the data model of ediarum.BASE.edit. DITA (rather than ODD) was chosen to enable this combination of ediarum.BASE.manual and the guidelines of edition humboldt digital. Furthermore, the internal DITA documentation includes not only the coding guidelines based on the specific material but also the specific Bedienungs instructions in ediarum.AVHR.edit.
The editorial guidelines refer to the corresponding sections of the DTABf documentation.

div.head: Schema
div.p: While the schema was initially formulated and maintained in RelaxNG, it is now available as a TEI-ODD file (Viglianti 2019) (from which RNG derivatives are still created). It is derived from ediarum.BASE.schema using ODD chaining, which in turn is derived from DTABf. This makes it possible to maintain and track the respective changes to the next “higher-level” schema at every level (ediarum, edition humboldt digital). The schema (both the TEI-ODD file and the RNG file) is published on GitHub.

div.head: Software & Technologies
div.p: The publication edition humboldt digital is created in ediarum from data entry through to publication. The digital work environment ediarum is a solution developed by the DH initiative TELOTA since 2012 that allows researchers to edit transcriptions of manuscripts, commentaries, and index entries in TEI-compliant XML, add textual and critical apparatus, and subsequently publish them on the web and as PDFs (Dumont/Fechner 2014). “ediarum” consists of several software modules that have been adapted for the creation of a digital edition. For data entry and editing in the “edition humboldt digital” project, the module ediarum.BASE.edit is used, which—as is customary with ediarum—is supplemented by a project-specific module ediarum.AVHR.edit. The ediarum.REGISTER.edit module is used to create and maintain the register entries. The exception is the bibliography, which is maintained in the reference management software Zotero; ediarum.DB provides a corresponding interface for synchronization.

Data is stored via ediarum.WEBDAV (Lampert et al. 2025), first in a Git repository (Fechner/Klappenbach/Lampert 2025) and, in a second (automated) step, in an instance of the open-source XML database existdb; the ediarum.DB module is also used here to manage the data. Existdb—together with the Jetty web server—serves as the basis for the digital edition, which was implemented using XQuery, XSLT, and XPath and is now maintained in an eXistdb app in accordance with the EXPath packaging specifications, simplifying deployment and development. The search functions utilize the Lucene-based faceting feature available since eXistdb 5.0. In addition, the edition features several custom-programmed caches that enhance performance, particularly for complex queries. The software digilib, developed at the MPI for the History of Science, is used to display the facsimiles, drawings, and illustrations.

This software stack was selected in 2015 because it has been used as the standard at the BBAW for editions in modern German studies since 2012. eXistdb has been in use in-house since the 2000s, and the ediarum input modules based on Oxygen XML Author have been in use since 2012. As a result, the TELOTA team possesses extensive expertise in these specific software tools and X technologies in general. In particular, ediarum (especially the module ediarum.BASE) is designed to enable the (further) development, deployment, and maintenance of software across projects. Ediarum had already been successfully deployed in several projects at the start of this initiative; it is now used in over 30 editorial projects—not only at the BBAW. The use of ediarum (and the technology stack as a whole) avoids siloed solutions and leverages synergies. This allowed the Editions project to build upon existing ediarum developments and to benefit from new functionalities developed for ediarum in other BBAW Editions projects—which, of course, also applies in reverse. Similarly, bug fixes in ediarum take effect simultaneously across all ediarum projects.

However, the “edition humboldt digital” was not able to benefit from all new ediarum developments. For example, the ediarum.WEB module is not used for the web presentation layer, as it was not developed until several years later. Migrating to it while retaining all features would have been too time-consuming. The use of TEI Publisher, which had already been released in early versions at the start of the project, was ruled out due to its rather limited functionality at the time. Consequently, the ehd was custom-built using XQuery/XSLT. Thus, the ehd—like many others—belongs to the category of “haute couture” editions, as Elena Pierazzo 2019 put it. This is also possible because the project is planned to receive funding for 18 years as part of the Academies Program. Apart from the lack of “prêt-à-porter” solutions at the start of the project, a “haute couture” solution for the ehd also seems sensible—if not necessary—given the scope and heterogeneity of the edited sources as well as the accompanying information (registers, chronologies, research articles, etc.).

div.head: Layout & Web Design
div.p: The design of edition humboldt digital is based on drafts that the author originally developed in 2014 for the project “Schleiermacher in Berlin 1808–1834.” Due to the fundamental similarity of the edition type and the genres of sources to be presented, the drafts could be reused and further developed for the ehd.

The design is based on the principles of “flat design,” i.e., simplicity, minimalism, and a strong focus on typography. The latter, in particular, is a central element, as this digital edition is primarily about one thing: text. For this reason, an Antiqua font (PT Serif) with a true italic style was chosen as the primary typeface. It is accompanied by a Grotesque font (PT Sans) from the same typeface family, which is used primarily in subnavigation menus, smaller-sized explanatory texts, and metadata. These klassischen typographic conventions—to the extent that they could be meaningfully adapted to the digital medium of the web—were also taken into account in the rest of the design. For example, a flexible text width that adapts to the width of the viewport was not used—in favor of a fixed width that roughly corresponds to the typographically recommended line length.

The design approach also deliberately omits a page header: To allow as much space as possible for the text, only a narrow navigation bar—which is clearly visible due to its black color—was placed at the top. Instead of the website title and sponsor logos (which were still quite common in 2014), the page header displays the document title or the title of the individual page. At the same time, this space also accommodates additional metadata and sub-navigation options (chronological browsing of letters; sub-section navigation; letters in the index, etc.).

The design faces two challenges: First, the abundance of different text types (edited letters, diaries, documents; research articles, and indexes) and information that needs to be accommodated. Here, the design follows the principle of not displaying everything immediately, but rather revealing certain information only in response to user interaction. There should always be sufficient white space to allow the eye to rest occasionally and to group and prioritize the various pieces of information in a meaningful way. A second challenge was (and remains) adapting the design to changing requirements and the ever-growing volume of material and information. With an Academy project of such long duration (2015–2032), not every type of information or function was foreseeable at the outset. Consequently, the design has been repeatedly adapted—from the introduction of a subnavigation menu, to the redesign of the homepage and the implementation of page-based text and facsimile displays, all the way to the edited texts, which are marked up with ever greater depth and complexity. Some of these changes were more successful than others. At the very least, Christian von Zimmermann praises the design of the research contributions: “[...] and this digital edition impressively refutes the frequently cited prejudice that it is not possible to present long texts in a digital medium in a readable and clear manner” (Von Zimmermann 2024, 292).

The 960 Grid System was used to implement the design in HTML, with heavy reliance on CSS. JavaScript is used only for specific—and, if necessary, replaceable—interface functions; the HTML pages are thus generated largely on the server side to facilitate archiving in the Web Archive or the BBAW’s web archive.

div.head: External Data & Web Services Used

figure.figDesc: The Networked Edition “Humboldt Digital.” Simultaneously published in the poster “The Networked Edition ‘Humboldt Digital.’” DH2023 in Graz. Abstract: https://zenodo.org/record/8107834.

div.p: For the digital edition, data from third-party projects was reused in several places, and external web services were utilized.

div.head: Cascaded Analysis Broker of the German Text Archive (DTA::CAB)
div.p: The standard search can be enhanced with a feature that also finds historical spellings and other word forms. For this purpose, the edited texts are linguistically analyzed and annotated using the DTA::CAB web service. Among other things, all words are lemmatized so that searches can be performed based on these lemmas. DTA::CAB was developed by Bryan Jurish as part of the German Text Archive.
For more information, see the documentation or visit Jurish 2012.

div.head: Humboldt’s Writings in the German Text Archive
div.p: Over 180 of Alexander von Humboldt’s works are available in full text in TEI-XML format in the German Text Archive. A feature has been implemented in the chronology that displays and allows searching of the title data for these works. This uses the D* OpenSearch API provided by the German Text Archive (see: OpenSearch Description). This allows users not only to view the full texts of Humboldt’s writings but also to search them: The search function enables users to specify the number of results and link directly to the results list.

div.head: Bibliography of Digitized Works on avhumboldt.de
div.p: As part of the avhumboldt.de portal, a bibliography of digitized works by Alexander von Humboldt that were published independently has been available since 2009 under the direction of Tobias Kraft. The data from this bibliography was converted to XML and integrated into the database at edition humboldt digital so that it can be displayed in chronological order.

div.head: correspSearch
div.p: The correspSearch web service aggregates machine-readable letter indexes from printed or digital editions of letters and makes them searchable in a centralized location (Dumont et al 2025; Dumont 2023, Dumont 2018). In addition, it offers an interface that allows this data to be queried automatically and reused in custom programs. Since Humboldt’s correspondence (Schwarz 2018) was already considered too extensive in the 1960s to be published in a complete edition, it has since been published in scattered volumes of correspondence or even in individual articles (primarily in the journal *Humboldt im Netz*) (Schröder 2008). For the first time, correspSearch brings together nearly all of the more than 7,000 published letters to and from Alexander von Humboldt and makes them searchable for research purposes.

In the “edition humboldt digital,” this data is queried via the correspSearch API in two places: first, in the chronology (when this option is enabled); this links the more than 1,600 entries on Humboldt’s life with his published correspondence. Second, the correspSearch API is queried in the individual view of a letter under “Explore Letter Network.” There, letters to and from Alexander Humboldt from other editions are retrieved to show which other correspondents Humboldt was in contact with during the respective time period. In addition, the system displays which letters each correspondent received and sent during that time period—the query is based on the GND or VIAF URIs stored in the registry. In this way, the “expanded correspondence context” of the letter network is made visible (Dumont 2023). This feature was originally developed as a prototype in the “edition humboldt digital” based on XQuery and subsequently reimplemented in the DFG project correspSearch as a freely reusable JavaScript widget csLink (Müller-Laackman / Dumont 2022). This widget is now also used in the “ehd.”

div.head: Practices of the Monarchy: Court Calendar
div.p: Also integrated into the chronology are events at the Prussian court in which Alexander von Humboldt participated and which are recorded in the Court Calendar, which is part of the publication “Practices of the Monarchy.” To this end, the TEI-XML data from the Court Calendar is imported into the edition humboldt digital, and mentions of individuals are mapped to the ehd register using GND URIs (if available; otherwise, they link to the register entries at Praktiken der Monarchie).

div.head: GeoNames & OpenStreetMap
div.p: The places and institutional locations listed in the register are generally assigned a URI from the open geographic database GeoNames. This allows the places to be identified across projects, which significantly simplifies the reuse of the data. The GeoNames URI is also used to retrieve the geographic coordinates, which—with the help of the open-source mapping service OpenStreetMap—enable a corresponding map to be displayed alongside the place and institution entries. This is particularly helpful for smaller locations visited during Alexander von Humboldt’s various journeys.

With version 11 of the “edition humboldt digital,” the geodata-based functions in the place index have been expanded: An interactive world map now provides an overview of all locations listed in the place index. In addition, for each individual location in its registry entry, neighboring locations that are also listed in the registry are displayed within a radius of approximately 30 km—both on the map and as a list with distance information (example: Zmeëvka).

div.head: Gemeinsame Normdatei & BEACON
div.p: Using the URI from the German National Authority File (Gemeinsamen Normdatei, GND) noted in an entry in the Person Register, additional data can be retrieved via the GND web service “Entity Facts.” On the one hand, “Entity Facts” are used to display portraits directly from Wikimedia Commons; since version 12 (2026), these portraits have also been used in a gallery as an additional way to access the Person Register. Additionally, information on relationships (family, friendships, etc.) between individuals is retrieved from the GND. This information is also automatically analyzed in the ehd using the GND URIs. With this data, users are automatically shown relationships between individuals included in the register (see, for example, the entry for Samuel Thomas Soemmerring).

The GND ID also makes it possible to link to other editions, encyclopedias, and projects relevant to the subject area of the “edition humboldt digital.” The BEACON interfaces of these projects are used for this purpose. For example, it is possible to identify thematic overlaps with other projects of the Center for Prussia-Berlin at the BBAW via the connections in the register data and make these available to researchers (e.g., Wilhelm von Humboldt or Friedrich Schleiermacher). External resources, such as Hidden Kosmos or Die deutsche Biographie, are also automatically linked in this way.

Since 2025, the retrieval of GND and BEACON files, as well as the functions based on them (portraits, links, etc.), have no longer been implemented exclusively in the ehd app but are gradually being replaced by the use of entityHub. The entityHub web service is currently being developed at the BBAW as a central service for BEACON and authority data aggregation (Dumont/Grabsch/Neuber 2026). See also the project page. One of entityHub’s goals is to centrally provide these data and functions—which are used in many of the BBAW’s digital editions—in order to consolidate development efforts and thereby significantly simplify maintenance.

div.head: Global Indexes for Scientific Names
div.p: The Plant Register (see above) uses various web services and APIs to automatically link scientific plant names from texts in the *edition humboldt digital* with corresponding entries in taxonomic databases. Using the Global Names Resolver web service, the Plant Register links scientific names to entries in the Encyclopedia of Life, Tropicos – Missouri Botanical Garden, and The International Plant Names Index (IPNI). In addition, the Catalogue of Life, the Biodiversity Heritage Library, and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility are queried via their own interfaces and linked accordingly. Additional databases may be added in the future, provided they have the appropriate technical interfaces.
Queries to the various databases and automated linking are based on the scientific plant name, which is encoded accordingly in the edited text and normalized where necessary.

div.head: DeepL
div.p: Starting with Version 12 (1 January 2026), the first sections of the *edition humboldt digital* will be automatically translated into English prior to publication. At present, this applies only to the chronology entries, as they are best suited for this purpose—being complete, concise, and written in modern German prose. For this purpose, the individual entries are sent as XML to the DeepL API via a script, and the result is saved. During translation, DeepL receives the TEI-XML structure of the snippets, ensuring that all markup (such as for people and places) is also preserved in the English version. A glossary and style rules are also applied when using the DeepL API.

The entries translated in this automated manner are marked with a corresponding note in the display. There are plans to have additional parts of the edition translated in this way in the future. Initial tests with edited letters yielded good results; however, the process becomes more challenging with texts that are more fragmented, such as travel diaries and documents. While the automatic translation of edited texts naturally carries risks, it would also significantly facilitate initial access to the texts for the highly internationalized field of Humboldt research.
However, the translations of edited texts that are currently available in individual cases have all been edited, revised, and reviewed.

div.head: Visualizations in the Chronology
div.p: Since Version 12 (1 January 2026), the Alexander von Humboldt Chronology has offered three visualizations. First, the homepage displays a so-called “heat map” that illustrates the distribution of the over 1,600 chronology entries. This allows users to better assess which time periods the chronology covers and to what extent. When a specific year is selected, the heat map changes to a bar chart showing the number of entries per calendar week.

Second, the chronology now offers a chronological-topographical view of a selection of Humboldt’s journeys in the form of a map on which the stops along the journey are marked. On the left-hand side, the journey is listed with additional date and location details; unlike the index entry, the location names displayed here are the contemporary names. On the right-hand side, the corresponding chronology entry is displayed based on the selected stop. Below this, links are provided to pages from edited travel diaries and letters in the ehd where the date of the day has been marked by the editors in TEI-XML.In some cases, the date is also mentioned in several travel diaries—not only in Humboldt’s own, but also in those of his traveling companions. This makes it possible, for the first time, to systematically access the travel diaries based on Humboldt’s itinerary.

Optionally, users can also display historical, often contemporary maps in addition to the travel route. In the case of the 1837 map of the Urals, it is even a map that was created, among other things, with the help of measurements by A. von Humboldt and was included with the report of his traveling companion Gustav Rose. These maps have been georeferenced using a GIS program based on multiple points, so they are generally located in the correct position on the modern map. However, due to the historical inaccuracies inherent in these contemporary maps, minor deviations may occur. On the other hand, the historical maps contain contemporary information (names, etc.) that is not found on the modern map, which is sourced from OpenStreetMap.

div.head: Reusing Location Comments
div.p: During the course of the project, it became apparent that it would be useful for the editors to be able to reuse a location comment. This would allow facts to be explained centrally while also being incorporated into other parts of the text. In the TEI-XML encoding, the location comment is created once as usual for this purpose. At all other locations, a reference to this comment can be easily made using the appropriate markup. In the ehd web interface, the comment is displayed accordingly at all linked locations. Additionally, such reused explanations list the pages where they have also been reused. This further reduces the burden on the in-text comment—even beyond the now-common linking of names, work titles, or glossary terms.

div.head: Data Provision & APIs
div.p: Data from the “edition humboldt digital” can be obtained via various interfaces as well as a complete TEI-XML dataset. Furthermore, various interfaces are available that allow other editions or portals to link to the “ehd.” This section provides information on this topic. Further details on this subject can be found in the article “Data on the Move,” published in the Journal of the Text Encoding Initiative (Dumont et al. 2026).

div.head: Licensing
div.p: The edition humboldt digital not only reuses external data and web services, but also makes its own data available under the open Creative Commons CC BY-SA 4.0 license via an interface and as a standalone data publication.

div.head: TEI-XML Interface
div.p: All edited texts, research articles, and chronology and index entries from the “edition humboldt digital” can be accessed via the TEI-XML interface at http://edition-humboldt.de/api/v1.2/tei-xml.xql (note version 1.2).

When accessed without parameters, a list of all data items is displayed, including the title and permalink of the respective current version. When accessed with the parameter type, a list of the respective document types is generated (see the table below). When accessed with the parameter id, the respective document is displayed.

div.head: Data Publication
div.p: All edited texts, research articles, and the indexes of persons, places, institutions, and abbreviations are also published as a complete TEI-XML dataset on edition humboldt digital. To this end, the texts and entries are not simply exported from the eXistdb, but are retrieved using an XQuery script via the TEI-XML API 2.0 of the ehd, so that the data structure matches that of the data accessible via the API. This allows for the incorporation of the enrichments found there (e.g., GNDs; URIs instead of IDs), the harmonizations with the DTABf, and the division of the register lists into individual TEI-XML files are utilized. The directory structure is also modified so that the data is organized by type (i.e., letters, diaries, research articles, register entries, etc.).

For initial, purely technical versioning, the TEI-XML files retrieved in this manner are uploaded to a Git repository, which is also publicly available on GitHub. After review and supplementation with the ehd’s TEI-XML schema (as RNG), the dataset is exported from there to Zenodo, where it is archived for the long term and made freely available: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.13752841 (canonical URL, always links to the most recent published version).

div.head: OAI-PMH
div.p: The metadata for the edited texts and research articles is made available via the interface https://edition-humboldt.de/api/v1.1/oai-pmh.xql?verb=Identify in accordance with the Open Archive Initiative’s Protocol for Metadata Harvesting. As a result, these texts are also automatically indexed in the Bielefeld Academic Search Engine (BASE). Currently, only Dublin Core is supported as the metadata format for OAI-PMH.

div.head: CMIF Interface
div.p: Through this interface, the correspondence metadata for all letters included in this edition can be retrieved in the Correspondence Metadata Interchange Format (CMIF). As a result, the letters edited in this edition are indexed in correspSearch.

The interface also already supports several extensions of CMIF v2. For example, it outputs the erwähnten persons as well as the URL to the respective TEI-XML full text. The latter makes it possible to search for and find these letters in full text within correspSearch as well (example: “fever*”).
URL: http://edition-humboldt.de/api/v1.2/cmif.xql

div.head: BEACON Files
div.p: The individuals present in the ehd database and tagged with a GND URI can be retrieved as a list in BEACON format via http://edition-humboldt.de/api/v1.2/beacon.xql and automatically linked to external digital resources. It is possible to restrict the list to individuals who are mentioned in the body of the letter or who are correspondents (see the table below).

div.head: Context Objects in span (COinS) & Zotero API
div.p: The bibliography entries are also accessible via APIs. On the one hand, they are embedded as machine-readable ContextObjects in SPAN tags on the HTML page at edition humboldt digital. This allows them to be imported directly into common reference management systems with a single mouse click. Additionally, the complete bibliography is available as a publicly accessible Zotero group via the Zotero API at https://api.zotero.org/groups/667230/items.

div.head: Versioning, Permalinks, and Citation Information
div.p: The texts and data provided at edition humboldt digital are maintained in versions, meaning that every published version (typically one per year) of the content is made available for retrieval. Versioning always applies to the entire published dataset. Consequently, the index entries also reflect the links of the respective version (see, for example, the entry for Georg Forster in Version 1 compared to Version 9). The version history, introduced with Version 8, provides an overview of the changes between the versions of edition humboldt digital. It also evaluates the number of edited pages, created chronology and index entries, as well as coded entity links, and visualizes them as bar charts. This is intended to document the ongoing work on the edited texts.

All texts are provided with both citation information and permalinks that reference the respective version (e.g., http://edition-humboldt.de/v1/H0002656; for information on citation and referencing in digital editions, see Bleier 2021). If necessary, edited texts can also be referenced by folio number by simply adding the folio number to the URL, e.g., https://edition-humboldt.de/v9/H0002656/2v. Research articles that do not have page numbers due to their “digital-born” nature, on the other hand, can be cited by paragraph. To do this, the paragraph number (which is always displayed in the upper left corner next to each paragraph) is appended with a # as a so-called fragment identifier, e.g., https://edition-humboldt.de/v9/H0016432#3. The use of Digital Object Identifiers (DOIs) was avoided, as they offer no real added value. On the contrary: since their registration is subject to a fee, they would incur significant costs (DOIs would have to be created for every page of the edited texts in every version, not to mention the registry entries) and would establish yet another layer of links alongside the existing permalinks, which would need to be maintained. Nevertheless, all measures to ensure the long-term availability of the ehd would still need to be implemented even if DOIs were used. For more on the issues surrounding DOIs, see also Arnold und Müller 2017. The TEI-XML dataset published on Zenodo, however, is assigned a DOI.

In addition, the individual texts and datasets are also assigned a canonical URL that always redirects to the most recent version. In this case, the version indicator is simply omitted from the path, e.g., http://edition-humboldt.de/H0002656. In addition to the texts and index entries, certain sub-sections (thematic focuses and various correspondences)—which, like a volume, are actually composed of multiple texts—are also provided with their own citation information, including canonical links (e.g., https://edition-humboldt.de/X0000003).

Thanks to the canonical and uniform URLs (“Humboldt” followed by a seven-digit number), it has also become possible for the printed volumes of the edition humboldt print to link back to their digital counterparts in the case of edited texts.

The interface itself—i.e., the XQL, XSLT, and JS scripts, as well as CSS and other files—is not currently versioned publicly. However, it is versioned and maintained in a Git repository for development purposes. Furthermore, there are plans for the future to additionally store and preserve every version of the digital edition (as an interface) in the BBAW web archive. To this end, the “edition humboldt digital” is already being technically prepared to ensure it can be archived as effectively as possible.
Separately, the data is also permanently published and archived on Zenodo (see the section “Data Publication”).
